content: African tick bite fever is an infectious disease caused by bacteria. The infection occurs when an individual is bitten by a tick carrying the bacteria. Symptoms typically manifest within two weeks following the tick bite. The initial sign is often a red sore at the site of the bite, which develops into a dark, crusted lesion known as an eschar. If multiple tick bites occur, multiple eschars may be present. As the disease progresses, additional symptoms may include fever, headache, muscle pain, swollen lymph nodes, and a rash. African tick bite fever is the most frequently reported tick-borne illness among travelers. Individuals traveling to sub-Saharan Africa, certain regions of the Caribbean, and Oceania (including Australia, New Zealand, Melanesia, Micronesia, and Polynesia) are at risk of contracting African tick bite fever. The risk is heightened for those engaging in outdoor activities such as camping, hiking, or game hunting in areas with dense vegetation, brush, or tall grass. Ticks carrying the bacteria are most active between November and April. Currently, there is no vaccine available to prevent African tick bite fever. Travelers can reduce their risk of infection by taking the following precautions: 1. Prevent Tick Bites: Be aware of tick habitats. Ticks are commonly found in grassy, brushy, or wooded areas, as well as on animals. Ticks can also be encountered in residential yards or neighborhoods. Treat clothing and gear with products containing 0.5% permethrin. Permethrin-treated clothing and equipment remain protective through several washes. Alternatively, pre-treated clothing and gear can be purchased. Use insect repellents registered with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) that contain active ingredients such as DEET, picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus (OLE), para-menthane-diol (PMD), or 2-undecanone. The EPA provides a search tool to help select the most suitable product. Always follow the instructions on the product label. Note that products containing OLE or PMD should not be used on children under three years of age. 2. Avoid Contact with Ticks: Steer clear of wooded and brushy areas with tall grass and leaf litter. Walk in the center of trails to minimize contact with vegetation. 3. Find and Remove Ticks: Inspect clothing for ticks after spending time outdoors. Ticks can be carried indoors on clothing. Remove any ticks found. To kill ticks on dry clothing, tumble dry them in a dryer on high heat for 10 minutes. If clothing is damp, additional drying time may be required. If washing is necessary, use hot water, as cold or medium-temperature water will not kill ticks. Examine gear and pets for ticks. Ticks can attach to clothing, pets, or equipment and later transfer to humans. Carefully inspect pets, coats, and backpacks. Shower promptly after outdoor activities. Showering within two hours of returning indoors can reduce the risk of tick-borne diseases. Showering may help wash off unattached ticks and provides an opportunity to check for ticks on the body. Perform a thorough body check for ticks. Use a hand-held or full-length mirror to inspect all areas of the body, paying particular attention to: Under the arms In and around the ears Inside the belly button Behind the knees In and around the hair Between the legs Around the waist If a tick is found attached to the skin, it should be removed as quickly as possible.
